tagline: Sandstone and volcanic rock mark the highway south to Kayenta.
intro: U.S. 163 passes rocks with very different origins south of Monument Valley. Agathla Peak is an eroded volcanic plug; across the highway, Owl Rock is a sandstone spire on the edge of Tyende Mesa. Both can be seen from the highway.

At Goulding’s, just outside Monument Valley in southern Utah, a trading post and home became a lodge. Harry Goulding sent photographs of the valley to John Ford, who made his 1939 movie Stagecoach and other Westerns there. The films helped popularize the area, and Goulding added lodging and other services.

Traveling south toward Kayenta, Mitchell Butte is another formation visible from Highway 163. Farther south, Agathla Peak and Owl Rock stand seven miles north of town. Kayenta brings the drive to the junction of U.S. 163 and U.S. 160, within the Navajo Nation.

moments.title: Goulding's
moments.text: A trading post became part of Monument Valley’s film history. Built in 1928, Goulding’s originally combined a store with the Gouldings’ home. During the Great Depression, Harry Goulding photographed the valley for director John Ford as Ford searched for a location for Stagecoach. Ford made that film here, followed by other Westerns; their popularity helped Goulding develop lodging and visitor services. The building was renamed and remodeled as tourism developed in Monument Valley. The trading post joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1980. In November 2023, the Navajo Nation purchased Goulding’s Lodge.

moments.title: Agathla Peak
moments.text: Agathla Peak rises more than 1,500 feet above the surrounding terrain, seven miles north of Kayenta. Its exposed rock is an eroded volcanic plug, made of volcanic breccia cut by dikes of minette, an unusual igneous rock. It belongs to the Navajo Volcanic Field of the southern Colorado Plateau. The peak is visible from U.S. 163. Across the highway, Owl Rock has a different composition: Jurassic Wingate Sandstone. Owl Rock stands on Tyende Mesa, where resistant limestone beds form ledges above slopes worn from softer siltstone. Owl Rock rises 1,000 feet above its surrounding terrain.
moments.notice: Look for Agathla Peak across the highway from the sandstone spire of Owl Rock.

moments.title: Kayenta
moments.text: Kayenta sits where U.S. 163 ends at U.S. 160. Its Navajo name, Tó Dínéeshzheeʼ, means “Fingers of Water,” referring to rainwater running down local rock formations. The township was established in 1986 under Navajo Nation law. Kayenta also names a chapter, a political division of the Navajo Nation whose territory extends into both Arizona and Utah. The chapter and the township are different geographic units. The township has a municipal-style government: an elected board of five members hires a manager to run it. It remains the only township under Navajo Nation law.
